title: Kerala NRI Panel Warns Job Seekers as Visa Scams Top Complaint List
excerpt: Over 30% of the 268 complaints received this year involve financial fraud built on fake work-visa promises, chairperson Sophy Thomas said.
body:
• More than 30% of complaints received by Kerala's Commission for Non-Resident Indians this year involve alleged financial fraud, including fake promises of work visas and overseas jobs.
  • Commission chairperson Sophy Thomas said the panel has received 268 complaints so far in 2026 and urged job seekers to use only NORKA-recognised recruitment agencies.
  • Investigators typically catch only middlemen while the real organisers escape, the commission said at an adalat hearing in Thiruvananthapuram.
  • The panel also flagged families pushed into debt for children's foreign education and bogus agents exploiting bereaved expatriate families over compensation claims.

Visa and job-recruitment scams dominate the grievances of Kerala's vast expatriate community, with more than 30% of complaints handled by the state's Commission for Non-Resident Indians (Keralites) this year relating to alleged financial fraud — including fraud built on promises of work visas and jobs abroad.

Commission chairperson Sophy Thomas disclosed the figures on Wednesday while addressing the media in connection with an adalat held at the Collectorate conference hall in Thiruvananthapuram. The commission has received 268 complaints so far this year, and nearly 75 were taken up during the adalat sitting.

How the scams work

"Most of the complaints received were related to visa recruitment fraud," Thomas said. "Job seekers should be careful to choose job opportunities only through NORKA-recognised recruitment agencies," she added, referring to the Non-Resident Keralites' Affairs department's network of approved recruiters.

The commission noted a frustrating pattern in enforcement: investigators looking into such scams usually end up tracking down only the middlemen, while the real culprits behind the rackets manage to get away.

A wider net of exploitation

The panel's warnings went beyond job fraud. Thomas highlighted the financial distress of families pressured into sending children abroad for higher studies without verifying whether the chosen universities are genuine. "Many young people come back and face the uncertainty of debts incurred for their travel and studies," she said, urging students to go abroad only with adequate means and to choose reputable institutions.

The commission also warned against bogus agencies and unauthorised legal advisers who exploit the families of expatriates who die or meet with accidents abroad — promising to help secure compensation the families are entitled to, then siphoning it off. Relatives seeking compensation should approach only lawyers recognised by Indian embassies, the panel said.

The official playbook against fraud

The warnings echo the central government's long-standing advisories. The Ministry of External Affairs has flagged a sharp rise in overseas job seekers being cheated by unregistered agents — often contacted only through WhatsApp or Facebook — who charge ₹2-5 lakh and provide fake offers, sometimes luring workers into dangerous conditions in East Europe, the Gulf, Central Asia, Israel, Canada, Myanmar and Laos.

The MEA's guidance: a genuine offer comes with an employment contract signed by the foreign employer, the agent and the worker, stating salary and terms; emigration must be on a work or employment visa, never a tourist visa. Under the Emigration Act, 1983, no agent may charge more than ₹30,000 plus GST as service charges, and every registered agent's licence number can be verified on emigrate.gov.in.

What job seekers should do

For Kerala's aspirants — and Indians everywhere eyeing Gulf or Western jobs — the checklist is short: verify the agent on emigrate.gov.in, insist on a signed employment contract before paying anything, never travel on a tourist visa for work, and route compensation claims through embassy-recognised lawyers. The commission's 268 complaints are a reminder that the fraud economy preys most on urgency and trust.

nri_angle: Kerala's vast Gulf diaspora is the prime target of these rackets; the commission's data shows visa fraud is now the single largest complaint category.
author: Diaspora Desk
